correspondence.component_scope: Chosen opening and northern Camas Valley Middle Fork corridor
correspondence.finding: The chosen northeastern opening is on the mapped Middle Fork Coquille River above Camas Valley. The labelled channel continues south past the Estes and Lake Creek junction setting and the western connection of Kinnan Reservoir into the Camas Valley collecting river. Kinnan Reservoir is depicted as a connected side water body; the selected generalized river corridor does not require an unsupported traverse across it. Its lower continuation and tributary joins remain visibly connected.

correspondence.component_scope: Southern Camas Valley and southwestern canyon transition
correspondence.finding: The named Middle Fork continues south through Camas Valley, receiving mapped side streams, then turns southwest along the confined highway-and-river valley toward the Rock Creek setting. The selected bends and joins stay in this continuous river corridor; no distinct headward feeder or interbasin transfer is imposed.

correspondence.component_scope: Western canyon, Rock Creek join and approach to Remote
correspondence.finding: The headward original continuously depicts the Middle Fork westward through the narrow valley, the Rock Creek joining setting and the northward turn toward Remote, where Sandy Creek joins. The strongly generalized east–west parts remain within that mapped collecting canyon rather than a separate drainage. The adjacent Camas Log Pond and small side ponds are not claimed as through-passages.

correspondence.component_scope: Remote–Bridge–lower Middle Fork corridor
correspondence.finding: The middle original follows the labelled Middle Fork from Remote through the successive valley bends, the Bridge settlement and lower canyon to the South Fork junction approach. Each selected part and connecting bend is covered by the continuous mapped river corridor. Named side creeks remain tributaries, not alternate names for the selected Middle Fork.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle Fork/South Fork join, Myrtle Point reach and North Fork confluence
correspondence.finding: The source depicts Middle Fork joining South Fork south of Myrtle Point, then South Fork continuing by Estabrook and the western side of Myrtle Point to the North Fork confluence. The receiving continuation is Coquille River. All selected joins are covered at corridor scale, without assigning an exact name-transition vertex to a generalized position. The association’s own prose independently places the major fork connections around Myrtle Point.

correspondence.component_scope: Receiving Coquille River through Norway and Arago to the fragment join
correspondence.finding: The middle and lower originals depict the main Coquille River continuously through the Norway–Arago floodplain and into the next selected fragment. The nearby Myrtle Point Log Pond and Johnson Log Storage and Sorting Reservoir are distinguishable side-waterbody settings; no unsupported managed transfer is required. Generalized selected bends correspond to the named river and its connected floodplain corridor.

correspondence.component_scope: Coquille town and broad northern lower-river bend
correspondence.finding: The lower original covers the preceding fragment join, the Coquille town reach, Cedar Point and the broad northwestern river bend. The main river is continuously depicted through the lowland and wetland setting; the selected straightened positions do not establish a separate cross-wetland diversion. Tributary creeks, floodplain sloughs and the side reservoir remain distinguishable from the receiving Coquille corridor.

correspondence.component_scope: Riverton–Parkersburg–Randolph lower valley
correspondence.finding: The named lower Coquille continues south through Riverton, rounds the broad valley bend and turns back northwest through Parkersburg and Randolph. The selected sequence follows this connected river-and-estuary corridor. The mapped Randolph Island and slough setting is covered without assigning every generalized position to a particular bank or minor parallel channel.

correspondence.component_scope: Prosper–Bullards and actual Bandon entrance-estuary ending
correspondence.finding: The lower original follows Coquille River past Prosper and Bullards into the widened Bandon estuarine water and its short Pacific entrance. The actual selected rendered ending lies within that connected entrance-estuary setting beside Bandon. The separately stored source endpoint and rendered endpoint are not treated as identical, and no extension of the selected line across the offshore ocean is asserted. The association’s own account independently identifies the river’s Pacific outlet at Bandon.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen inland-ice opening and south-southeastward upper course
correspondence.finding: The complete chosen opening and both long upper stored parts lie in the national original’s continuous inland-ice terrain. The selection proceeds south-southeast across the mapped ice-cover and sub-ice topographic compilation toward the exposed-rock belt. The map covers the full opening and the join between the two long parts; its contour and lineament symbols are not natural-river evidence.

correspondence.component_scope: Southern ice turn
correspondence.finding: All five short parts carry the selected corridor farther south through the mapped ice-covered region to its southern turn. The continuous original accounts for each join and the turn beside the inland edge of the nunatak/bedrock belt. No glacier name or surface/subglacial water connection is inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastward transition into the nunatak belt
correspondence.finding: The eastward bend and short rising turn enter the mapped ice/nunatak setting. The original shows the ice margin and successive exposed-rock projections around this whole interval. Every stored part and its connection with the upper southern turn is covered; the modeled line itself is not independent river evidence.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle ice and exposed-bedrock passage
correspondence.finding: The middle eastward passage crosses the original’s alternating ice-covered spaces and exposed geological bodies. The selected corridor, rather than a continuously drawn natural stream, corresponds to this terrain mosaic. The entire interval and all joins are in the inspected original; no lake or managed connector is positively identified.

correspondence.component_scope: Northeastward lower bend across the rock and ice mosaic
correspondence.finding: The lower northeastward bend, short eastward links and local back-and-forth turn are all accounted for in the same uninterrupted national map. They traverse the exposed-rock/ice-margin setting around elongated bedrock bodies. The geological colors and blue inland-ice symbols are not assigned lake, glacier or river identities.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastward approach and southeastward coastal turn
correspondence.finding: The final eastward links and ensuing southeastward turn approach the inner coastal bedrock and narrow ice passages. Each stored part and internal join is within the inspected map area, with the adjacent narrow marine-inlet setting visible beyond the coastal rock margin. No exact glacier or receiving-fjord name is established.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual final stored part and terminal setting
correspondence.finding: The whole final part, its bend and actual selected ending were inspected in the enlarged original locality. At ordinary map scale the ending lies in the inner coastal rock/ice-margin setting beside the head of a narrow marine inlet; the receiving coastal-water context is also covered. This does not place the endpoint precisely on the historical shoreline or ice front, establish a surveyed river mouth, or identify a particular glacier or fjord. The supplied sea-terminal class is retained as model metadata only.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen southwestern opening and northeastward lowland feeder
correspondence.finding: The opening lies in a cultivated and partly wooded lowland containing narrow drainage ribbons, field drains and several separate stream traces. Imagery establishes that setting and the northeastward approach, but not a sufficiently clear selection-specific through-connection to the named collector. Kijewski's independent field-study prose distinguishes the piedmont dispersal/tatucal setting from the lower river system; its ungridded Croquis 1 does not resolve this particular opening. No exact feeder name is assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: First joined lowland collector and wetland-adjacent northward passage
correspondence.finding: The imagery shows the selected northward collector in one continuous lowland corridor with incoming channels, wet patches and abandoned meanders. The regional hydrography identifies the lower Escalante system in this position. Patch cloud and channel simplification limit local detail but do not introduce another missing regional interval. This downstream correspondence does not settle the preceding feeder connection.

correspondence.component_scope: Winding middle plain and approach to the town-side branch
correspondence.finding: The overlapping upper and middle views show the north-trending meandering river belt, intervening bends and joined reaches across the agricultural plain. The selected generalized line remains in that continuous river corridor, including older meander traces beside the more conspicuous channel. Exact active-bank positions are outside the finding.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern town-side reach and Santa Bárbara–San Carlos passage
correspondence.finding: The selected reach turns northeast from the middle river toward the eastern town corridor, then passes through the Santa Bárbara–San Carlos setting. The imagery distinguishes this narrower river ribbon from the conspicuous western channel/dike route, which is not substituted for the selected path. The independently authored 2009 field-report introduction identifies the river connecting these twin towns as Escalante. Channel engineering is accounted for geographically; construction date and present diversion operation are not inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower northward reach and eastward wetland approach
correspondence.finding: The lower image follows the selected river north of the towns and through its eastward turn, among cultivated parcels, riparian vegetation and wetland margins. The chosen river continues toward the northeastern mouth; separate southern and western waterways remain distinct and are not used to replace selected reaches.

correspondence.component_scope: Final meandering wetland reach and actual lake terminal
correspondence.finding: The final selected reach corresponds to the visibly continuous meandering channel through the lake-margin wetland and its northeastern mouth. It reaches Lago de Maracaibo. No additional open-sea reach is implied by the retained model's sea terminal class, and no neighboring river mouth is substituted.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen northeastern opening and southwestward headward approach
correspondence.finding: The chosen opening lies in the northeastern feeder valley of the upper Évora corridor. The municipal relief map and the state sheet depict its southwestward approach into the south-running valley above Palmarito de la Sierra. Original imagery exposes the same narrow mountain drainage and the widening downstream valley. The directly named upper Évora course continues from this setting; the separate eastern drainage toward Surutato is not substituted for the chosen approach.
correspondence.name_scope_limit: Representative upper-corridor attribution, not a surveyed official source point or a claim that a name label is printed at the first selected vertex.

correspondence.component_scope: Palmarito de la Sierra, upper joins and San Benito descent
correspondence.finding: The selected course follows the continuous north–south valley past the Palmarito de la Sierra surroundings and descends toward San Benito and La Huerta. The state original directly prints Río Évora on this corridor. The municipal map distinguishes the eastern Arroyo Grande and El Potrero approaches, and the imagery shows their joining setting within the same valley. The selected route continues down the Évora rather than crossing the intervening upland to the eastern Surutato drainage.
correspondence.name_scope_limit: Incoming named approaches are context only and are not assigned as names of the selected main course. Palmarito de la Sierra is a locality, distinct from the separately mapped Palmarito waterway farther west.

correspondence.component_scope: Westward turn, Mocorito and western lowland joining sector
correspondence.finding: Below the San Benito–La Huerta sector, the route turns west across the foothill plain toward Mocorito. The municipal relief original repeats Río Évora along the westward river; its linework separates the Los Chinos approach from the selected northern course. The state original and overlapping imagery expose the successive bends and the river plain at Mocorito, including the north-side joining channel and the westward continuation toward the reservoir. There is no unviewed transfer between the upper valley and this receiving river.
correspondence.name_scope_limit: Mocorito's locality label and the table's R. Mocorito basin designation are not, by themselves, evidence of a hydronym synonym.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern reservoir approach and Presa Eustaquio Buelna passage
correspondence.finding: The Évora approach west of Mocorito leads into the eastern arm of the waterbody explicitly named Presa Eustaquio Buelna on the state sheet and P. Eustaquio Buelna in the municipal original. The selected westward and northwestward bends enter the connected storage setting and then approach its southwestern outlet beside Guamúchil. The map, waterbody symbol and original imagery agree on this passage. Northern reservoir arms and their tributaries remain separate from the selected eastern entry.
correspondence.name_scope_limit: The reservoir proper name is distinct from Río Évora. No present water level, shoreline, dam operating rule, turbine route or precise selected structure is asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Reservoir outlet, Guamúchil and southern lowland continuation
correspondence.finding: The Salvador Alvarado relief map directly labels Río Évora at the reservoir's southwestern outlet and continues it along the Guamúchil urban margin into the southern plain. The state original and imagery show the river corridor leaving the storage setting and proceeding southwest, with sinuous river reaches distinguishable from straighter irrigation works. This supplies ordinary reservoir-outlet and urban-passage correspondence without assuming that every selected point falls in the current wetted channel.
correspondence.name_scope_limit: The principal irrigation system is not renamed Évora, and present distribution of water between river and managed channels is unverified.

correspondence.component_scope: Alhuey–Angostura agricultural plain and managed crossings
correspondence.finding: The same river corridor continues past the Alhuey–Angostura surroundings and south through the cultivated plain. The Angostura original traces the sinuous Évora separately from named canals including La Esperanza, Nacozari and Humaya. Its linework and the two overlapping images cover the selected turns and intermediate managed crossings. These are connected river-plain passages, not an assumed lateral jump from an isolated channel merely because both lie in the Mocorito basin.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Évora, embanked coastal ground and actual terminal
correspondence.finding: The Angostura relief map directly labels the lower Évora and carries it to the northeastern margin of the connected Santa María coastal water, east of El Calcetín and northwest of Punta Santa María. The original imagery shows the selected southwestward approach entering a modified wetland margin with rectilinear embankments and pond blocks, then reaching the tidal-channel/open-water setting at the actual selected end. This terminal is inside the coastal receiving system; it is not an invented direct outlet across the outer Pacific barrier. The historically mapped river corridor and present photographic receiving setting are continuously covered.
correspondence.name_scope_limit: The terminal corridor includes substantial artificial modification. Évora is not assigned to every embanked ditch, pond or tidal branch. No exact present river mouth, bank, flow through an individual pond cell or permanently open sea inlet is claimed.
